parts.title: Part 3: Water, waste and tanks
parts.summary: How the fresh, grey and black tanks work, how to read the panel, how to dump without clogging, where a sewer smell really comes from, and how to keep clean water and dry floors.

sections.title: RV holding tanks: fresh, grey and black explained

blocks.html: Every RV has three tanks. One holds the clean water you use. Two hold the water you have used. The two waste tanks are kept separate on purpose, and confusing which is which causes most of the trouble that follows.

head: Tank
What it holds
What it is for
rows: Fresh
Clean potable water
Sinks, shower, toilet flush, drinking
Grey
Drain water from the sinks and the shower: soap, food scraps, grease, hair
Holding used wash water until you dump
Black
Toilet waste: urine, faeces, toilet paper
Holding sewage until you dump

blocks.html: The two waste systems are separate. The grey-water system takes wastewater from the sinks and the shower. The black-water system takes sewage from the toilet. Each tank has its own control valve, and both drain through a common sewer hose.

The fresh tank is separate from both. It feeds the freshwater system including the water heater, faucets, and toilet when the coach runs on city water. The toilet is a fixture that uses fresh water. It is not an inlet to either waste tank; it drops its contents into the black tank.

The distinction matters for two reasons. First, only black waste carries the clogging, odour, and septic hazards, so only the black tank needs the careful habits in the sections below. Second, most parks let you leave the grey valve open while you are parked, but almost none let you leave the black valve open.
You can often leave the grey tank valve open while hooked to a sewer connection, but some parks require both valves closed at all times. Check the rule where you are parked.

sections.title: RV tank sensors reading wrong, and what to do

blocks.html: The wall panel is not a gauge. It is a set of lights that step up in thirds. The vertical columns for fresh, grey, and black water show fluid levels in roughly one-third increments. So the panel reads empty, one-third, two-thirds, or full. Treat it as a rough warning light, not a measurement.

Most panels use conductive probes set through the tank wall. A probe lights when liquid bridges the gap between that probe and a ground sensor lower down. The problem is that anything conductive coating the probe does the same job. Waste film, toilet paper, soap scum, and mineral scale all bridge the circuit, so a tank that is empty can read as full and a tank that is full can read as empty.

Tank sensors mainly fail because of a buildup of waste inside the tank. Failed electronics, broken or unattached connector wires, or failed reading boards can also cause misreads, but it is almost always thick, sticky waste built up in the tank. In black tanks that is human waste and dissolved or broken-down toilet paper. In grey tanks it is moulds and mildews growing in the hot, moist environment.

There is a simple physical check on a direct-drop toilet, which is one whose bowl empties straight into the black tank. Holding tank gauges are seldom accurate, so use a flashlight and look down from above the stool to judge how full the tank is.

That trick does not work on a macerator or vacuum toilet. Those designs do not open a straight path into the tank, so there is nothing to look at. On those, you rely on the panel and on your own sense of how long the tank lasts.
Low water is often called the number one contributor to sensor fouling. Water level and waste buildup drive the readings more than the electronics do.

sections.title: How much water to put in your RV black tank

blocks.html: A black tank is meant to hold a mix of solids and liquid, not solids alone. Water is what lets the tank empty. When the tank is mostly liquid, the rush of draining water swirls the solids out through the valve and the hose. When the tank is dry, solids sit on the plastic, harden, and stay.

The rule that keeps water in the tank is to leave the black valve closed except when you are dumping. Keeping the gate valve closed at all times while you use the coach leaves enough liquid in the tank for a smooth flow through the gate and the drain valves when you dump. The liquid causes a swirling action that takes accumulated solids with it. Keeping the valve closed even when hooked to a sewer connection stops solids from building up in the tank.
You also start the tank wet, before first use. Fill until there is at least one inch of solution directly under the toilet. The solution is water mixed with an odour-controlling chemical.

You dump when the tank is well filled, so the volume of liquid does the flushing. Drain the tanks only when they are at least three-quarters full, which gives enough water to flush waste materials completely out of the drain lines and hose. If a tank is less than three-quarters full, add enough water to get a full flush.

The safe minimum is half a tank: leave the black tank valve closed and dump when it is half or more full. Dumping with less than half a tank seldom gives enough volume to flush solids, and can leave a persistent paper and faecal build-up.
So the practical window is somewhere between half and three-quarters full, plus a wet start. The exact number is a habit, not a specification.

There is no standard gallon figure for the black-tank pre-charge. Published figures are depths or descriptions: at least one inch of solution under the toilet, or enough water to cover the bottom of the tank so waste residue cannot harden. Never dump the black tank until it is three-quarters full. Keep an inch of water in the bowl to stop tank odour entering the living space.

The widely repeated figure of five gallons is a starting rule, not a specification. A common method is to run the flush until it clears, close the black tank dump valve, then add at least five gallons of fresh water back into the tank. Some treatments are marketed at three to five gallons, and owners report anything from about five to ten gallons. The right number depends on the size of the tank.

sections.title: The RV poop pyramid: how it forms and how to avoid it

blocks.html: The pyramid is a cone of solids and paper that builds up under the toilet drop and hardens. It forms because liquid leaves the tank while solids stay. Each flush adds a little more solid on top, and the pile grows.

The usual cause is leaving the black valve open at a full-hookup site. With the valve open, liquid drains away continuously. The solids have nothing to float in, so they settle and dry. Keep the gate valve shut and the swirling liquid carries the solids out.
Keep the valve closed and dump when the tank is at least half full, because a low-volume dump will not flush solids.
A leaky gate valve causes the same result more slowly: waste water leaks out and leaves solids behind to build up and solidify on the floor of the tank, which can block the tank outlet.

The single habit that prevents a pyramid is keeping the black valve shut. A tank that always holds liquid cannot stack solids, because waste that lands in water spreads out instead of stacking on dry plastic.

sections.title: RV black tank chemicals: what to use and what never goes in

blocks.html: A bottle sold for black tanks is usually one of three things: a deodoriser that masks or suppresses smell; an enzyme or bacterial treatment meant to break down waste and paper; or a formaldehyde-based steriliser, often called blue chemical, that kills the bacteria causing odour.

The best-documented harm is to the park's system, not your own tank. Avoid any chemical toilet product that lists formaldehyde as an ingredient in any concentration. Formaldehyde kills the bacteria that break down waste in septic tanks, so holding-tank waste containing it can kill the bacteria in a septic tank and eventually clog the system.
Some states go further: tanks containing formaldehyde or similar chemicals must not be disposed of into an on-site sewage disposal system. Formaldehyde waste can be refused at a park dump.

Bleach is the other common harm, and it damages your own equipment. Never use bleach to treat or sweeten a tank: it can severely and quickly damage valves, seals, and gaskets. Use only enzyme-based or bacterial-based products, and note that the term biodegradable does not necessarily mean a product is safe for humans or the environment. Do not use chlorine or caustic chemicals such as bleach or drain openers in the toilet, because they damage the seals in the toilet and the dump valves.

Against all of this, a treatment is optional. Water does the heavy lifting. A good product may help with odours and waste breakdown, but plenty of RVers manage without one. Treat odours as a clue: a tank additive cannot repair a dry toilet seal, blocked vent, leak, clog, or dirty tank.

The rule on what goes in is narrow. Never put anything in the holding tanks other than normal drain water, body waste, and biodegradable products. Paper wrappers, gum, and cigarettes, no matter how small, should never go into either the grey or black tank, because they can damage the plumbing or the tanks.

The item most often named as a clog cause is the disposable wipe sold as flushable. Any paper that does not break down does not belong in the tank. Bleach, chlorine, and drain openers are also excluded, because they damage seals and dump valves, and formaldehyde additives should be avoided.

Whether enzyme and bacterial treatments help or hurt is disputed. Some recommend them; others argue digesters turn the tank into a septic tank and create the sludge that fouls sensors. The question is not settled. What is settled is that water, a closed valve, and correct dumping matter more than any bottle.

Whether coffee grounds, cooking grease, or septic-treatment packets are formally banned by manufacturers is not established. The rule language is general, covering only normal drain water, body waste, and biodegradable products.

sections.title: How to dump your RV tanks in the right order

blocks.html: Dumping is a fixed sequence. Do it the same way every time and the hose stays clean and the valves keep working. The black tank guide covers the whole job, including the chemicals and the flush.

items: 1. Connect and lock the sewer hose at both ends before you touch any valve.
2. Confirm both gate valves are closed. Crack the cap only when you are ready to attach the hose.
3. Optionally run grey for a few seconds first, to leak-test the fittings.
4. Open the black valve fully and let it drain.
5. If the coach has a black-tank flush, run it with the black valve open until the clear fitting runs clear.
6. Close the black valve.
7. Open the grey valve and let it run. This scours the hose.
8. Close the grey valve, disconnect, cap, and rinse the hose.

blocks.html: The order is black first, then grey, and the reason is the hose. Draining the black tank first lets the grey water wash the black residue from the drain lines and hose. When the black tank is drained, drain the grey tank immediately to flush the black water from the sewer hose. The last thing through the shared hose is the cleaner grey water.

When both tanks are empty, flush them with a freshwater rinse before you close the valves. Do not open a holding-tank gate valve when the protective cap is installed on the pipe. If you open a valve with the cap still on, you dump the tank into the cap and onto yourself.
Be sure the gate valve is open when flushing the tank. The flush water needs somewhere to go.

Why not leave the black valve open. With the valve open at a full-hookup site, liquid drains as it arrives and solids stay behind and dry, which is how a pyramid forms. The grey valve is a different case, and some manufacturers and parks allow it to stay open. Black stays closed.
Dump when the black tank is between half and three-quarters full. Whenever possible, drain both holding tanks before travelling.
The standard outlet is a three-inch bayonet. A clear elbow at the hose end lets you see when flow stops and when rinse water runs clear.

sections.title: RV sewer smell inside: why it is usually not the tank

blocks.html: Grey water is not clean and not sterile. It carries soap, food, grease, and hair, and because it is rarely flushed, it can smell as bad as black water, or worse.
When a smell appears inside, look somewhere other than the tank first.

The first suspect is a dry P-trap. Each sink and the shower has a water trap that seals tank gas out of the living space. These traps must have water in them to trap odours. When the vehicle is moving, water can splash out of the sink and shower drains, and when it is stored, the water can evaporate, letting odours into the vehicle. If that happens, run water from the faucet into the drain to refill the traps.

The second suspect is the air admittance valve, a one-way vent on the drain that lets air in so the P-trap is not siphoned dry. When water flows through the P-trap, the valve opens to let air into the pipe and closes when the flow stops. If the valve does not close fully, odour permeates the area around the sink and spreads through the interior. A failed valve is cheap and simple to replace.

items: Smell strongest inside a sink cabinet: suspect the air admittance valve or a loose fitting there.
Smell strongest at the drain: suspect a dry or siphoned P-trap. Run water down it.
Smell anywhere, and the toilet bowl will not hold water: suspect the toilet seal.
Smell with none of the above: suspect a blocked roof vent, which can push odour back through the plumbing.
Only after all of those check out: the tank itself is the likely source, and the fix is cleaning and correct dumping, not another bottle of deodoriser.

blocks.html: A smell is confusing because it travels. Gas entering at one fitting can be noticed somewhere else entirely. Work from the cheapest checks upward: refill the traps, then test or replace the admittance valve, then check the toilet seal and the roof vent.

sections.title: How to sanitise your RV fresh water tank

blocks.html: Filling the fresh tank may have no automatic shut-off. Watch the monitor panel while filling. Excess water vents from an overflow in the vent pipe onto the ground when the tank is full, which prevents the tank from rupturing if it is overfilled. An overfilled fresh tank runs onto the ground through the vent rather than bursting. It will not flood the inside on its own, but you should not walk away from a fill. Some high-end coaches have auto-fill, so check your own manual.

Sanitising means putting a measured dose of chlorine into the fresh system, letting it sit, then flushing. The target is 50 parts per million. Use a solution of one gallon of water and half a cup of chlorine bleach (5% sodium hypochlorite), and add one gallon of solution for every 15 gallons of tank capacity. That mix puts a 50 ppm residual chlorine concentration in the water system. Let the solution stand for at least four hours, then drain and flush. To remove the chlorine taste, use a solution of one quart of vinegar to five gallons of water. Tiffin warns: "Concentrations greater than 50 ppm might damage the water lines and/or the tank."
The same recipe and limit are standard: one gallon of solution per 15 gallons of tank capacity, and no more than 50 ppm.

Recipes conflict on the bleach amount. Half a cup of bleach per 15 gallons and a quarter cup per 15 gallons are both published, which is a two-to-one difference. Household bleach has become stronger over time, from about 5.25% to between 6% and 8.25% sodium hypochlorite, so the same volume now makes a stronger mix. The safe instruction is to compute to about 50 parts per million using the percentage printed on your jug, and not to exceed it.
One more step: remove the coach water filter before disinfecting the fresh-water system, because the filter will remove the chlorine.

Do not borrow the cistern recipe. Emergency cistern disinfection uses a much stronger mix, three cups of unscented bleach per 100 gallons, which is roughly three times the RV dose per gallon. The 50 ppm RV limit exists to protect the lines and the tank; the cistern strength is not for a potable RV system.

A drinking-water hose is for drinking water only. Use a hose manufactured and labelled for potable water service; these are usually white. Do not use a garden hose, which is not made for drinking water and can leave a plastic or rubber taste.
Keep a second hose for the black-tank flush, and never swap them. Do not use the same hose for filling the fresh tank and for the flush, and do not use potable drinking-water hoses for flushing.

City water arrives at whatever pressure the park supplies, and that varies. If city water pressure is more than 60 psi, use a water pressure regulator to prevent damage to the coach. A regulator screws onto the supply and holds the pressure down.

Plumbing systems are usually tested to about 100 to 125 psi, but to avoid warranty problems some manufacturers recommend only 40 to 50 psi, and a safe cap is 60 to 65 psi. Follow your own manual's limit. Park pressure varies for real reasons: wells, booster pumps, elevation, and demand change through the day. Owners report anything from the mid-30s to 60 psi and higher, which is why a regulator is worth carrying.
Fit the regulator at the spigot or pedestal end rather than at the coach inlet, so the hose is protected too.

A whole-coach filter has limits. As installed, the filter removes chlorine, dirt, and other matter, but it is not guaranteed to remove the tastes and odours of iron and sulfur. Change it every 6 to 12 months depending on the quality and quantity of water used. Filters also cost flow: a small in-line filter restricts flow more than a 10-inch standard canister, and a standard canister is more restrictive than a jumbo canister. A filter plus a cheap regulator is a common cause of a weak shower.

sections.title: How RV water damage happens, and how to avoid it

blocks.html: Almost every flooded RV traces back to one of five situations. Each has a mechanism and a habit that avoids it.

1. City water left on with a leaking fixture and nobody watching. This is the big one. On city water the system is under pressure continuously. Any leak, whether at a toilet valve, a supply fitting, or a cracked line, keeps running until someone closes the spigot. Turn off the city water whenever you are outside the coach, and fifty gallons of water will do as much damage as 500. If you want pressure while away, use the onboard pump and tank instead.

2. A stuck toilet fill valve. The toilet is the highest-consequence leak, because an overflow lands in the living space. A solenoid valve stuck in the open position keeps water flowing into the bowl, and a bowl can overflow on city water if the toilet valve is not seated. After each flush, watch the bowl until the water stops. Install a quarter-turn shut-off valve at the toilet if there is no factory one. Shut off city water when you leave.

3. Fresh-tank fill left unattended. There may be no automatic shut-off when filling. The tank overflows out a vent rather than bursting, but an unattended fill still wastes water and can flood a wet bay. Never walk away from a fill. If your coach has an automatic fill, use a flow meter.

4. Winter freeze damage that becomes a spring flood. A cracked fitting or cracked water-heater tank shows up as a hidden leak the first time you pressurise in spring. The habit: winterise fully, and inspect before you pressurise. Winterising is covered in the next part.

5. Backflow through the pump check valve. A stuck pump check valve can let city water backfill the fresh tank and overflow it. This is usually an overflow rather than an interior flood, but it is common. Cycle the pump with a faucet open, or fit a second inline check valve.
One test catches a slow toilet leak: leave water in the bowl and check it an hour later. If the bowl has drained, the seal or the valve is the problem.

parts.title: Part 4: Cold, heat and storage
parts.summary: What cold breaks and in what order, how to winterise and where half-jobs fail, what four-season really means, and how to stop condensation and mould.

sections.title: What freezing does to an RV, and in what order

blocks.html: Water expands as it freezes, and some parts of the plumbing cannot stretch. PEX tubing, the flexible plastic pipe used for most RV water lines, survives a modest amount of expansion. The fittings, valves, faucet housings, the pump, and the water heater cannot. Water heater tanks, or the heat exchanger lines in tankless designs, cannot either. A single freeze can do the damage, and it often is not visible until you pressurise the system in the spring.

Parts exposed to outside air freeze before parts tucked inside the heated shell. Those are the low-point drains, the city water and tank flush inlets, outside showers or kitchens, and the water heater.

The order in which things freeze follows that logic: exposed first, protected last. A common ranking is exterior hookup hoses, then low-point drains, then belly-pan plumbing, then holding tanks, then interior plumbing if heat fails.

The components named again and again as freeze points are PEX lines, plastic fittings and elbows, faucets and shower valves, toilet valves, outside shower assemblies, water pumps, water heaters, filter housings, low-point drains, the city-water check valve, washer and ice-maker lines, and the black-tank flush line.
The water heater is the most expensive failure. Residual water in the tank freezes, expands, and cracks it, and the whole tank then needs replacing.

sections.title: How to winterize an RV: the two methods, and the half-jobs that still freeze

blocks.html: There are two ways to winterise an RV, and both are in service of the same thing: getting every drop of water out of a system that will freeze and split. Which one suits your coach, how much antifreeze it takes, what pressure a blow-out runs at, and the order to work in are all in the winterising guide, which is the full job. What follows is the shape of it.

head: Method
How it works
Where it fails
rows: Wet (antifreeze)
RV antifreeze is pumped through the lines until it replaces the water
Leaves nothing to freeze if done fully, including the traps and the water-heater bypass
Dry (blow-out)
Compressed air pushes the water out of the lines
Can leave water in toilet valves and traps; still needs antifreeze in the traps

blocks.html: Blow-out leaves a risk that antifreeze does not. The blow-out method can fail in freezing temperatures because it cannot always remove all the water from sensitive parts such as modern toilet water valves. The options rank as: blow-out risky, antifreeze good, a combination of antifreeze and blow-out best.
Half-jobs that still freeze:

items: Blow-out without antifreeze in the P-traps. Compressed air flows through pipes but does not lift standing water out of a trap. Skipping this is a common cause of freeze damage in supposedly winterised RVs. Even blow-out advocates add antifreeze to the traps, because blowing out the supply lines removes most of the water but antifreeze still protects the P-traps and toilet.

Bypassing the water heater without draining it. Bypass keeps antifreeze out, but water left inside still freezes and can crack the tank. Bypassing the water heater without draining it first is a common mistake. Draining the water heater during winterising is a must.
Forgetting the exposed fixtures. The outside shower, outdoor kitchen, black-tank flush line, city-water check valve, and washer or ice-maker lines each hold water that can freeze.

sections.title: What a four-season RV actually means

blocks.html: Four-season is a marketing term. No standards body defines or tests it. The fire and life safety standard for RVs, NFPA 1192, does not define four-season or all-season. Its scope is fire and life safety criteria for recreational vehicles, and its purpose is to provide protection from loss of life from fire and explosion. Its chapters cover administration, referenced publications, definitions, general requirements, fuel systems, fire and life safety, plumbing, and vehicular requirements. There is no climate, insulation, or season chapter.

The industry association RVIA does not define it either. A certification run by the parts maker Truma claims to add credibility to a four-season label, but it is Truma's own single test, using a cold chamber at minus 15 degrees Celsius and measuring how long the coach takes to warm to 20 degrees, and it is not a general industry standard. ANSI defines no four-season standard either; its RV-related standards cover park model RVs, low-voltage systems, and exterior ladders.

Manufacturers rarely test RVs in freezing conditions, and a four-season sticker on an RV may not mean much. There is no RV industry standard that sets apart extreme-weather RVs from competitors; how a manufacturer defines four-season is entirely up to the company.

Manufacturers use their own names for their own feature bundles: terms such as four-season, Arctic Protection, Climate Shield, and Polar Package. Four-season capability is not just about staying warm; these RVs should also handle the extremes of a mid-summer heatwave. Not many manufacturers will confidently stand behind a single R-value for their entire RV. Because there is no test, read features, not labels. A useful tell is whether the maker itself claims four-season or something weaker. One maker, Lance, describes its package as being for the shoulder seasons, which is not a deep-winter claim.

There is no published pass or fail test a buyer can cite. If a seller says a coach is four-season, the question to ask is what the features are: an enclosed and heated underbelly, ducted furnace heat to the tanks, dual-pane windows, and insulation values for the roof, floor, and walls. A label is not a measurement.

sections.title: RV underbelly insulation and heated tanks

blocks.html: The four-season features that matter most are the ones that keep the tanks and pipes warm.

head: Feature
What it does
How much it matters
rows: Enclosed, heated underbelly
Seals and warms the space around tanks and pipes
The main marker of a real cold-weather package
Ducted furnace heat to tanks
Routes warm air to tanks, valves, and lines
Strong; uses the furnace you already run
Tank heating pads only
Electric pads warm the tanks
Weaker; needs shore power and does less in deep cold
Dual-pane windows
Two layers with an air gap
Helps with heat loss and condensation, but not magic in an RV

blocks.html: An enclosed and heated underbelly is closed in and warmed, usually by furnace ducts or by 12-volt or electric heating elements, to protect the tanks, valves, and plumbing from freezing. Ducted heat routes warm air to the holding tanks and valves, sometimes with tank pads or heat tape added; on one maker's version, ducted heat is routed into individually insulated holding tanks to keep the tanks, valves, and PEX lines warm. Dual-pane windows are two layers of glass or acrylic with an air gap; they improve R-value, reduce drafts, limit condensation, and cut outside noise.

Heating pads alone are the weaker substitute. An enclosed, ducted underbelly uses the furnace you are already running. Tank heating pads need shore power and do less in deep cold. Many campers marketed as four-season RVs do not have enclosed underbellies.

Insulation has to be everywhere to work. A year-round coach needs insulation in the roof, floor, walls, front cap, and slide areas, not just one or two highlighted zones. Dual-pane windows help but are not magic in an RV, because RV units are built differently from house units.

Even a well-built coach has limits. RV walls, ceilings, and floors will only ever be so thick, which makes it nearly impossible to rival a residential house, and even the best winter set-up will fail if it is not used and maintained properly and within the manufacturer's stated limits. A coach used in a North Dakota winter needs skirting, a heated water hose, and active heat management; the same coach on the Gulf Coast is barely stressed. The owner who spends the winter in North Dakota must do more to protect the coach than the owner who travels to warmer coastal air.

sections.title: RV condensation: why it forms and how to stop it

blocks.html: Condensation forms when warm, moist air inside meets a cold surface, such as window glass, a thin wall, or a metal frame. The moisture in the air turns to liquid on the cold surface. RVs are small and tightly sealed, so the air inside loads up with moisture quickly.

People are the main source. With normal activities such as breathing, cooking, and bathing, a family of four can release up to three gallons of water vapour into the air each day. Without proper ventilation or a dehumidifier, that moisture condenses on cooler surfaces, potentially damaging belongings and the RV itself. The cold surfaces are worst in cold weather, because the temperature gap between the inside air and, for example, a single-pane window is largest then. Cooking, showering, and drying clothes indoors add moisture fast.

items: Ventilate while you cook and shower. Run the range hood and the bathroom fan, and open a window a crack when the outside air is colder and drier than the inside air.

Use a dehumidifier when the outside air is warm and damp, because then opening windows brings moisture in rather than pushing it out. If condensation persists despite ventilation, a dehumidifier can help manage excess moisture.
Wipe down wet windows and frames so the water does not run into the walls.
Leave cabinet and closet doors partly open so air can move, which keeps those spaces drier.
Use a desiccant only in a sealed, unoccupied space such as a closed cabinet, and refresh it as directed.

blocks.html: Sealing a coach completely does not stop condensation; it can make it worse, because trapped moisture has nowhere to go. The goal is to move moist air out or to dry it, not to lock it in.

sections.title: How to store an RV, short term and long term

blocks.html: Mould needs three things: moisture, a food source, and a moderate temperature. Mould can develop in any environment with moisture and temperatures between 40°F and 100°F. The food source is ordinary dirt and dust, which is why a clean, dry coach stores better than a dirty one.
The control lever is humidity. Keep indoor relative humidity below roughly 50 to 60%, and ideally between 30 and 50%.

Short-term storage, meaning weeks between trips, is mostly about drying out. Empty and dry the black and grey tanks, run water into every P-trap, and leave a vent or window cracked for airflow. If the coach sits in sun, expect interior heat to drive moisture out of soft furnishings by day and condense it at night, so ventilation matters more than in a house.
Long-term storage, over a winter, adds the freeze work from earlier in this part: full winterising, water heater drained, traps filled with antifreeze. On top of that:

items: Clean the coach before storage. Crumbs, grease, and dust are the food mould needs.
Dry it thoroughly. Wipe wet surfaces and let soft furnishings air out before closing up.
Leave cabinet and closet doors partly open for airflow.
Keep some ventilation. Do not seal the coach completely, because trapped moisture raises condensation. Completely sealing an RV without ventilation can actually increase condensation inside.
Use a dehumidifier or desiccant as appropriate. A powered dehumidifier needs power; desiccant packs suit a sealed, unpowered space and should be refreshed every 30 to 60 days.
Fix leaks before storage. A small roof or window leak over a winter is a mould start.

blocks.html: When moisture is bad enough to grow visible mould over a large area, that is a remediation job rather than a wipe-down. Visible mould over about 10 square feet is the usual threshold between a do-it-yourself clean and professional remediation.
